title: DAVID’S SISTER ABIGAIL HAD A SON NAMED AMASA—And His Father Is Described Differently Across Biblical Texts
paragraphs: DAVID’S SISTER ABIGAIL HAD A SON NAMED AMASA—And His Father Is Described Differently Across Biblical Texts

One verse calls Amasa’s father Ithra “the Israelite.” Another calls him Jether “the Ishmaelite.” Then David looks at Amasa and says, “You are my bone and my flesh.” This is not a detail to hide from. It is an invitation to open the Bible more carefully—and discover that God’s Word is not afraid of the questions we are sometimes afraid to ask.
There are names in the Bible we race past.
Names buried inside genealogies.
Names we pronounce badly, skim quickly, and forget five seconds later.
Abigail.
Amasa.
Jether.
Ithra.
To most readers, they look like background characters standing quietly behind David, Absalom, and Joab.
But slow down.
Because hidden inside this family is one of those details that can make an attentive Bible reader stop mid-sentence.
And once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
David had a sister named Abigail.
Not Abigail the wife of Nabal who later became David’s wife. This is another Abigail.
David’s own sister.
First Chronicles places her directly inside Jesse’s family:
“And their sisters were Zeruiah, and Abigail.”
Then comes the detail almost nobody talks about:
“And Abigail bare Amasa: and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmeelite.”
—1 Chronicles 2:16–17, KJV
The Hebrew of 1 Chronicles 2:17 reads:
וַאֲבִיגַיִל יָלְדָה אֶת־עֲמָשָׂא וַאֲבִי עֲמָשָׂא יֶתֶר הַיִּשְׁמְעֵאלִי
Wa’avigayil yaledah et-‘Amasa, wa’avi ‘Amasa Yeter hayYishme‘eli.
In straightforward English:
“Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.”
The final Hebrew expression is especially important:
הַיִּשְׁמְעֵאלִי — hayYishme‘eli
“The Ishmaelite.”
So Abigail, David’s sister, had a son named Amasa.
That makes Amasa part of David’s extended family.
It also means something else.
Joab was not simply Amasa’s military rival.
Joab’s mother Zeruiah was Abigail’s sister.
Amasa and Joab therefore belonged to the same close family network.
These were not strangers meeting on a battlefield.
This was family.
Blood.
History.
Loyalty.
Ambition.
Political fracture.
And eventually...
murder.
But before we reach the blood on Joab’s sword, there is something unusual sitting quietly in another biblical passage.
Turn to 2 Samuel 17.
David’s son Absalom has rebelled against his father. Jerusalem has been shaken. David has fled. The kingdom is tearing itself apart.
A son is trying to take his father’s throne.
Friends are choosing sides.
Families are being divided.
People who once stood beneath the same banner are preparing to kill one another.
And Absalom needs a commander.
Not Joab.
Amasa.
Second Samuel 17:25 says in the traditional Hebrew textual form that Amasa was the son of a man named יִתְרָא — Yitra, usually rendered Ithra, and describes him as:
הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי — hayYisre’eli
“the Israelite.”
That is why the King James Version reads:
“...whose name was Ithra an Israelite...”
—2 Samuel 17:25.
Did you catch it?
Chronicles:
Jether the Ishmaelite.
Samuel’s traditional Hebrew text:
Ithra the Israelite.
Same Amasa.
Same mother.
But a variation in the father’s name and, more strikingly, in the description attached to him.
This is where some Christians become nervous.
Don’t.
You do not honor Scripture by pretending textual questions do not exist.
And you do not protect the Bible by being afraid to examine the Bible.
Faith does not require intellectual dishonesty.

The Hebrew forms Yeter—Jether—and Yitra—Ithra—are closely related forms of the name, and modern translations commonly recognize the connection. The more significant textual question is “Israelite” versus “Ishmaelite.” First Chronicles 2:17 clearly reads “Ishmaelite,” while the Masoretic Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 17:25 reads “Israelite.” Yet some manuscripts of the ancient Greek Septuagint also support “Ishmaelite” in Samuel, which is why several modern English translations either render Samuel accordingly or place the variation in a footnote.
That matters.
It means we should not casually announce, “The Bible contradicts itself,” as though no textual history exists.
But neither should we manufacture an explanation and call it certainty.
The honest answer is better.
There is a genuine textual variant here.
Some ancient witnesses preserve “Israelite.”
Others support “Ishmaelite.”
Chronicles independently identifies Amasa’s father as Jether the Ishmaelite.
Bible translators have to examine those witnesses and decide how the text should be represented, which explains why you can open different English Bibles and see different wording in 2 Samuel 17:25.
And this should teach us something beautiful about reading Scripture.
God never commanded you to be frightened by difficult verses.
Read them.
Study them.
Compare them.
Ask questions.
Look at the Hebrew.
Look at the Greek witnesses when textual questions arise.
Study the manuscript evidence.
And have enough humility to say:
“I do not know everything yet.”
Because sometimes the strongest faith in the room is not the person shouting that there is no question.
Sometimes it is the person holding an open Bible saying:
“I have a question, but I am not walking away from Jesus.”
Maybe somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Because perhaps you have questions you have been terrified to admit.
Perhaps someone told you that asking questions means you lack faith.
Perhaps you encountered a difficult passage online and quietly panicked.
Perhaps an atheist showed you a textual variant.
Perhaps a skeptical friend asked something you could not answer.
And something inside you whispered:
What if my faith cannot survive this?
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ is not threatened by your investigation.
Truth does not become less true because you examined it.
The Scriptures themselves have come down to us through a rich manuscript history, and responsible study sometimes requires recognizing places where ancient witnesses differ.
But the story of Amasa becomes even more haunting when you stop staring only at the textual question and start watching the man.
Because Amasa was standing inside a broken royal family.
His cousin Absalom rebelled against David.
Amasa became commander of Absalom’s army.
Imagine that.
David’s own nephew leading the forces of David’s rebellious son against David.
Family fighting family.
Blood against blood.
A kingdom collapsing beneath ambition, betrayal, wounded relationships, and sin.
Does that sound ancient to you?
Or does it sound painfully modern?
Maybe your family has never fought over a throne.
But perhaps they fought over an inheritance.
A marriage.
Money.
A betrayal.
A rumor.
A funeral.
A business.
A piece of land.
Something somebody said twenty years ago and nobody ever truly forgave.
Maybe people who once ate at the same table now refuse to sit in the same room.
Maybe cousins became enemies.
Maybe siblings stopped speaking.
Maybe someone betrayed someone, somebody chose sides, and eventually everyone forgot how the war even began.
That is what sin does.
It does not merely break rules.
It breaks people.
It breaks homes.
It breaks trust.
It turns tables into battlefields and relatives into rivals.
And Amasa was standing right in the middle of one of those families.
Then Absalom died.
The rebellion collapsed.
And David had every political reason to look at Amasa and see a traitor.
Amasa had commanded the army of the son who tried to steal David’s kingdom.
He had stood on the wrong side of the rebellion.
He had every reason to expect rejection.
Maybe punishment.
Maybe death.
But David sent him a message.
And the words are staggering:
“Art thou not of my bone, and of my flesh?”
—2 Samuel 19:13.
My bone.
My flesh.
David was essentially saying:
You are still family.
Then David promised Amasa the position of commander in place of Joab.
A rebel commander was being offered restoration.
A man who had stood against the king was being brought near the king.
Do you see where this begins to touch something deeper?
Amasa is not Jesus.
David is not a perfect picture of Christ.
We should never force biblical characters into allegories Scripture does not explicitly make.
But the pattern of rebellion, mercy, reconciliation, and restoration inevitably reminds the Christian reader of something far greater.
Because we were not merely confused people trying to find God.
Scripture says sin made us rebels.
We wanted God's gifts without God's rule.
His creation without His authority.
His blessings without His holiness.
His heaven without His throne.
Yet the Gospel announces something almost impossible to believe:
The King came looking for rebels.
Jesus Christ did not wait for humanity to repair itself.
He entered our world.
He carried our sin.
He went to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And sinners who repent and trust in Christ are not merely tolerated.
They are reconciled.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Brought near.
That is grace.
Not God pretending rebellion never happened.
Grace looks directly at the ugliness of sin and says the blood of Jesus is sufficient for the repentant sinner.
Maybe your scandal is different from Amasa’s.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe everybody does.
Maybe your worst decision has followed you for years.
Maybe people still introduce you in their minds by the thing you did.
The divorce.
The addiction.
The affair.
The lie.
The prison sentence.
The abortion.
The pornography.
The betrayal.
The season you walked away from God.
The years you wasted.
The person you hurt.
The ministry failure.
The secret nobody knows.
And somewhere deep inside, you have wondered:
If people knew everything about me, would they still believe God could use me?
The Gospel does not answer by telling you your sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
But the Gospel also refuses to tell you your sin must have the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
Repentance is coming home to reality.
It is finally dropping the defense.
Finally opening the locked room.
Finally saying:
“Jesus, I did it.”
“I sinned.”
“I cannot cleanse myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
And grace answers the repentant sinner with something scandalous:
Christ has already paid what you could never pay.
But Amasa’s story still has one brutal turn left.
David’s promise placed Amasa where Joab once stood.
And Joab was not a man who surrendered power easily.
Later, when Amasa came to meet him, Joab approached him with words that sounded almost tender:
“Art thou in health, my brother?”
Then Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand as though to kiss him.
Family language.
A familiar gesture.
A moment that looked safe.
And concealed beneath it...
a weapon.
Joab struck Amasa.
Amasa fell.
And the man David had intended to restore lay dying in the road.
The story is horrifying because betrayal usually hurts most when it comes wearing a familiar face.
Some of you understand that without explanation.
The person who wounded you was not an enemy.
That would have been easier.
It was someone who knew your name.
Someone who knew your weaknesses.
Someone you trusted.
Someone who called you brother.
Someone who hugged you.
Someone who prayed beside you.
Someone who knew exactly where to place the knife.
And perhaps you survived physically...
but something inside you has been bleeding beside that road ever since.
Hear this carefully.
Jesus does not command you to pretend evil was good.
Forgiveness is not calling betrayal harmless.
Forgiveness does not mean refusing appropriate boundaries or justice.
But bitterness cannot resurrect what was taken from you.
Hatred cannot heal you.
Revenge cannot redeem your story.
Only Christ can enter wounds that deep without becoming another wound Himself.
Jesus knows betrayal.
Judas did not approach Him screaming hatred.
Judas approached with a kiss.
Christ knows what betrayal feels like when it arrives through someone close.
He knows abandonment.
False accusation.
Mockery.
Violence.
Blood.
And yet at the cross, evil did not get the final sentence.
Resurrection did.
That is why your story does not have to end at the place where somebody wounded you.
Your failure does not get the final sentence.
Your family history does not get the final sentence.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence.
Jesus Christ does.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is imaginary.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes rebels and makes them sons and daughters.
He takes the guilty and washes them.
He takes the ashamed and clothes them in righteousness.
He takes people hiding in darkness and calls them into light.
He takes what Satan intended to use as your permanent identity and makes it part of the testimony of what Christ rescued you from.
So maybe you came here because the headline surprised you.
David had a sister named Abigail?
She had a son named Amasa?
Why does one biblical text say Israelite while another says Ishmaelite?
Those questions brought you through the door.
But perhaps God wanted to confront a deeper question before you left:
What are you still hiding from Jesus?
Not from Facebook.
Not from your pastor.
Not from your spouse.
Not from your family.
From Jesus.
What have you been defending that He is asking you to confess?
What wound have you been feeding instead of surrendering?
What bitterness have you renamed “discernment”?
What secret sin have you renamed “struggle” because calling it sin would require repentance?
What rebellion have you learned to explain instead of forsake?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Sit with it.
Pray.
Open your Bible.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to know that Jesus still restores broken people.
Not because every sentence is unforgettable, but because there may come a night when you need to remember this truth again:
Questions do not frighten Christ.
Your wounds do not repel Christ.
Repentance does not disqualify you from grace.
And your past does not possess authority greater than the blood of Jesus.
If Gospel Warrior has helped you grow closer to Christ, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.

Christian giving should never be manipulated, and salvation, prayer, grace, and access to Christ are never for sale. Your local-church responsibilities and your personal convictions about tithes and offerings should be honored faithfully before God.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a purchase of God's favor.
It is an opportunity to participate in the work.
But even if you cannot financially support it, you can still help.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone.
Help put biblical truth in front of one more person.
But before you leave, remember Amasa.
Remember the name buried inside the genealogy.
Remember the textual detail that made you stop.
Remember the family ripped apart by rebellion.
Remember the king calling a former enemy “my bone and my flesh.”
Remember the betrayal disguised as affection.
Remember the blood beside the road.
Then look beyond David.
Beyond Amasa.
Beyond Joab.
Look toward another King.
A King betrayed with a kiss.
A King wounded by sinners.
A King crowned with thorns.
A King nailed to wood.
A King whose blood was spilled not because His enemies defeated Him, but because He willingly gave His life to redeem sinners.
And then remember the empty tomb.
Because Christianity does not end with blood on the ground.
It ends with a risen Christ.
So bring Him the question.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the rebellion.
Bring Him the family wound.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish you could tear out.
Repent where you have sinned.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Seek truth without fear.
Walk in the light.
And trust the Savior whose grace is greater than the chapter you thought had ruined everything.
Because sometimes the page you wanted erased becomes the very page where people finally see how powerful the grace of Jesus really is.
